title: Of presumption
hook: he describes his own faults with honesty and humor (Essays 2.17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cat. Your line was who's playing whom. Did an animal, or a person, turn out to be running the game? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

I work too hard. I care too much. I'm a perfectionist. Ask someone to name their flaws, and sometimes this is what comes back: a boast wearing a disguise. Montaigne answers the question for real, in an essay he calls Of Presumption, and he doesn't disguise a thing. He goes through his faults the way you'd go through a junk drawer, holding each one up to the light, and some of them are funny.
screen: `I WORK TOO HARD.` → `A BOAST IN DISGUISE.` → `MONTAIGNE ANSWERS FOR REAL.`

segments.voice: First, what presumption is. Montaigne says it has two sides: thinking too highly of ourselves, and thinking too little of others. He says his own lean runs the other way. He tends to prize what others have and undervalue what's his. Second, the list. He says he's shorter than average, and counts it a real drawback. His body was strong but clumsy at the skills a gentleman was supposed to have. Dancing, tennis, wrestling: he says he was no good at them. His hands were so awkward that he couldn't read his own handwriting. He says he couldn't properly fold a letter, carve meat at the table, or saddle a horse. No excuses come attached. Third, the one thing he's proud of. Is there anything he does prize in himself? Yes: his judgment, his good sense. And then the joke lands on him. That's the one quality, he points out, that nobody in the world thinks they're short of. So even his pride is ordinary. Fourth, plainly, with a smile. This isn't self-hatred. He isn't groveling for reassurance, and he isn't fishing for compliments. He's being accurate, and he's being amused. That's the mix: a person who can describe his own faults the way he'd describe the weather. On an ordinary Tuesday, my faults, plainly sounds like I'm bad with dates instead of I'm a terrible friend. True, specific, survivable, and maybe a little funny.
screen: `TOO HIGH ON SELF, TOO LOW ON OTHERS.` · `CLUMSY HANDS, BAD HANDWRITING.` · `PROUD OF WHAT EVERYONE THINKS THEY HAVE.` · `ACCURATE, AND AMUSED.` · then, large: `MY FAULTS, PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: describe one fault kindly. Sit, and let the breath settle. Choose one real fault of yours. Not the worst thing about you; something ordinary. Now say it to yourself in one plain sentence, the way Montaigne would. No excuse at the front, no attack at the end. I lose my keys. I interrupt when I'm excited. I put things off. Hold that sentence for a while. If something about it is a little funny, let it be funny. The bell holds the time.
Of presumption. Montaigne's essay on thinking too much of ourselves, in which he lists his own faults, clumsy hands and all, honestly and with a smile. Today's word.
Your line: my faults, plainly. Today, when a fault of yours shows up, name it in one plain sentence, without a speech for the defense or the prosecution. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Presumption as a model for honest self-description: naming faults plainly, neither boasting nor groveling, and keeping a sense of humor.

fork.setup: you're writing a book about yourself that strangers will read. you've reached the part about your shortcomings. what does Montaigne do?
options: skip it and list his achievements.
list them plainly: short height, clumsy hands, handwriting he can't read.
write that his only fault is working too hard.
fork.reveal: he lists real faults, specific and a little funny, and then turns the joke on his one point of pride: good sense, which nobody thinks they lack.

trapdoor: what you thought: an essay scolding proud people.
what it means: an honest self-measure, faults included, with neither boasting nor groveling.
what a scholar hears: Montaigne gives presumption two sides, valuing ourselves too much and others too little, says he leans the other way, and offers his list of faults as the evidence.
